analysis.investment_thesis: Aarti Drugs fails both legs of the Magic Formula — earnings yield of ~7.2% (EBIT 290 Cr / EV ~4,018 Cr) is well below my 12% threshold, and ROCE of 13.1% is far short of the 20%+ I require for a quality business. The combination of contracting earnings and heavy capex with poor FCF conversion makes this uninvestable on quantitative grounds.
key_strengths: Moderate leverage (D/E 0.39) with 5/5 years of positive operating cash flow — decent balance sheet discipline
High promoter holding (55%) provides alignment; diversified API portfolio across anti-infectives, NSAIDs, antidiabetics
Long operating history since 1984 with international sales presence reducing single-market risk
key_risks: EBITDA has collapsed from peak 490 Cr (FY21) to 307 Cr (FY25) — a 37% decline with no recovery in sight
Capex of 177 Cr in FY25 against FCF of just 67 Cr; CWIP ballooned to 261 Cr in FY24, indicating heavy capital consumption with poor returns
Revenue declined two consecutive years (2,716→2,529→2,387 Cr) amid margin compression — operating margin a thin 6.16%
red_flags: ROIC/ROCE of 13.1% — well below Greenblatt's 20% floor, meaning capital is being consumed faster than value is created
Earnings yield of ~7.2% (EBIT 290 Cr ÷ EV ~4,018 Cr) — not cheap enough to compensate for poor business quality
Operating income CAGR 9Y of only 5.4% while net profit CAGR 9Y is 10.4% — divergence suggests one-time items and non-operating income distorting reported profits
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula: Enterprise Value = Market Cap 3,408 Cr + Debt 615 Cr − Cash 5 Cr = ~4,018 Cr. EBIT (Operating Income) FY25 = 290 Cr. Earnings Yield = 290/4,018 = 7.2% — well below my 12% hurdle. ROCE (proxy for Greenblatt ROIC) = 13.1% — below the 20% minimum for a "good" business. Both legs of the formula are weak simultaneously, which in my ranking system would put Aarti Drugs near the bottom of the investable universe.

The operational story reinforces the numbers: the FY21 spike in profitability (EBITDA 490 Cr, net profit 280 Cr) was a COVID-era windfall, not structural quality. Since then, the company has invested aggressively — capex totaling ~720 Cr over FY22–25 — yet EBITDA is down 37% from peak and revenue is actually shrinking. This is capital destruction, not capital compounding. At P/E 16.8x with declining earnings and a 6% operating margin, the stock is neither cheap nor high-quality. I need both.
